title: The Sharpe Pint: Capex Hangovers and Midnight Tariffs

opening_mood.text: Morning. If you spent Friday afternoon staring at your screens hoping for a quiet slide into the weekend, the macro gods had other ideas. Between Donald Trump pulling a midnight tariff rabbit out of his legal hat, Alphabet and Intel giving the market a severe case of AI capex anxiety, and the US-Iran conflict keeping oil desks on high alert, it has been a proper shift.

Grab a coffee (or a very early pint, we won't judge). Today we are unpacking why Google is burning cash for the first time since its IPO, how to ace your next M&A interview by avoiding the 'WACC Fallacy', and a clever PyTorch trick to stop your quantitative models from choking on monthly macro data. Let's get into it.

content.text: Trump's Section 301 Workaround: A 10-12.5% Tax on 60 Economies

The US has slapped new Section 301 tariffs ranging from 10% to 12.5% on imports from 60 of its largest trading partners, effective Friday, 24 July 2026. The official justification from US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer is that these countries have failed to effectively enforce bans on goods made with forced labour. This replaces the Section 122 levies that expired early Friday morning.

Why does this matter? It covers a staggering 99.4% of US imports. Legally, it is a direct response to the Supreme Court's February 2026 ruling (Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump), which declared that the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) does not authorise the president to levy tariffs. Blocked by the courts, the Trump administration pivoted to Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974. While Canada and Mexico are exempt under the USMCA, the EU and other major trading partners are fully in the firing line. The UK remains at the 10% rate secured by Keir Starmer last year, which ironically now puts British businesses at a relative disadvantage compared to the EU, which previously enjoyed a better deal.

The City Angle: This is a massive supply-chain and inflation story. It layers on top of existing tariffs, meaning cumulative duties are stacking up. Importers have a tiny grace period until 28 July to manage in-transit goods. For asset managers, this means modelling margin compression for consumer goods and manufacturing, and preparing for a sticky inflation print that might tie the Fed's hands.

items: What to say at work: 'The pivot to Section 301 forced-labour tariffs is a clever legal workaround after the Supreme Court's IEEPA ruling, but it effectively acts as a blanket 10-12.5% tax on global trade. Expect margin compression in consumer-facing equities and a headache for central banks trying to cut rates.'

content.text: Alphabet's Capex Shock: Google Burns Cash for the First Time Since 2004

Alphabet reported Q2 2026 earnings, and despite spectacular headline numbers, the stock fell roughly 7% over the next two trading days. Revenue grew 24% to $119.8 billion and Google Cloud surged 82% to $24.8 billion. However, capital expenditures doubled year-over-year to $44.9 billion, pushing free cash flow into the red at negative $5.9 billion. This is the first time since its 2004 IPO that Google has recorded negative free cash flow.

The headline GAAP EPS of $9.11 was heavily distorted by a $99 billion paper gain on equity stakes in Anthropic and SpaceX. Strip that out, and the cash flow reality is stark: Google is spending more on AI infrastructure than its core search engine can throw off. To make matters worse, full-year 2026 capex guidance was raised to a massive $195-205 billion range.

The City Angle: The 'AI capex debate' is no longer theoretical. Hyperscalers are spending like regulated utilities, and the market is punishing them for it. This is a classic 'show me the ROI' moment. If Google is burning cash, the pressure on Microsoft, Meta, and Amazon to prove their AI spend is generating actual cash flow is now immense.

items: What to say at work: 'Alphabet's print is a watershed moment. For twenty years, Google was the ultimate cash machine. Now, it's burning $5.9 billion in a single quarter to fund AI infrastructure. The 82% Cloud growth is impressive, but when you're raising 2026 capex guidance to $200 billion, the market is going to demand immediate, tangible revenue, not just paper gains on Anthropic stakes.'

content.text: Intel's AI Turnaround: The CPU Strikes Back

Intel reported Q2 2026 earnings, and its stock initially jumped nearly 5% in after-hours trading, providing a rare bright spot in a brutal week for tech. Q2 revenue was $16.1 billion (up 25% YoY, its fastest growth since 2011), beating the $14.3 billion consensus. Adjusted EPS was $0.42, doubling the $0.21 estimate. Crucially, its Q3 revenue forecast of $15.8 billion to $16.8 billion shattered Wall Street's $15.1 billion estimate.

Intel's Data Center and AI segment surged 59% YoY to $6.3 billion, driven by massive demand for its Xeon 6 CPUs and AI accelerators. CEO Lip-Bu Tan (who took over in March 2025) confirmed that its advanced 18A manufacturing node is in volume production with yields tracking ahead of expectations. Intel also raised its 2026 capex forecast to over $20 billion, signalling customer-driven confidence.

The City Angle: This is a massive relief for the semiconductor sector and a sign that the AI build-out is lifting boats other than just Nvidia. If they can successfully execute the 18A node volume ramp, Intel becomes a viable domestic foundry alternative, which is a major geopolitical hedge for US tech.

items: What to say at work: 'Intel's Q2 print is the first real sign that Lip-Bu Tan's turnaround plan is working. A 59% jump in data centre revenue shows that the AI infrastructure build-out isn't just an Nvidia story—CPUs are seeing a massive second-wave demand. If they can successfully execute the 18A node volume ramp, Intel becomes a viable domestic foundry alternative.'

content.text: Volkswagen's Profit Slump: The Chinese EV Threat Hits Home

Volkswagen reported a 9.5% drop in Q2 operating profit to €3.5 billion (missing estimates of €4.3 billion) and slashed its full-year 2026 revenue outlook. It now expects sales revenue to decline by up to 3% this year, reversing its previous forecast of up to 3% growth. Shares fell over 3% on the news.

VW is facing a brutal sales slump in China (deliveries fell 6.3% in H1) and intense competition from cheap Chinese EV brands like BYD and Geely entering Europe. In response, CEO Oliver Blume is pushing a radical restructuring, proposing to double job cuts to 100,000 and potentially close four German factories—a move facing fierce union opposition.

The City Angle: This highlights the structural crisis in European manufacturing. High energy costs, regulatory burdens, and a slow transition to EVs are leaving legacy giants exposed. For automotive credit and equity analysts, the focus is entirely on whether Blume can break the power of the German unions to push through these existential cost cuts.

items: What to say at work: 'VW's profit warning and the threat of 100,000 job cuts show that the Chinese EV threat is no longer a future risk—it's an active crisis. Oliver Blume is trying to force a bloated, union-heavy legacy carmaker to operate like a lean tech company, but closing German plants is a political landmine. It's a textbook case of structural margin compression.'

content.text: SAP's Cloud Backlog Boom: Calming the AI-Doom Narrative

SAP reported Q2 2026 results, with cloud revenue up 22% to €6.28 billion and its current cloud backlog jumping 27% to €22.9 billion. The stock jumped over 6% in Frankfurt, providing a rare bright spot in a jittery week for tech. This is a crucial data point for software equity analysts.

SAP's stock had been down 35% this year on fears that generative AI would 'hollow out' the enterprise software subscription model. The strong backlog growth proves that customers are still committing to long-term enterprise contracts. However, SAP did trim its 2026 profit guidance slightly to reflect the dilutive impact of its recent acquisitions of data firm Dremio and AI startup Prior Labs.

The City Angle: This suggests that enterprise software isn't dead; rather, companies are integrating AI directly into their core databases (like SAP's Business Data Cloud, which was in 90% of its top 50 deals). It's a win for the 'AI-enablement' thesis over the 'AI-disruption' thesis.

items: What to say at work: 'SAP's backlog surge is a massive sigh of relief for software investors. The narrative that AI would instantly disrupt enterprise ERPs was overblown. Instead, SAP is successfully embedding AI into its existing databases. The minor profit guidance cut for acquisitions shows they are paying up to stay ahead, but the underlying demand is clearly there.'

content.text: American Express: Reinvesting the Beat (and Annoying the Street)

American Express reported Q2 2026 earnings, beating EPS expectations ($4.53 vs $4.40 expected) and raising its full-year revenue growth guidance to 10%. However, the stock fell over 5% on Friday as the market reacted to unchanged earnings per share guidance.

The market was disappointed that Amex held its full-year EPS guidance steady at $17.30 to $17.90. CFO Christophe Le Caillec explained that they are choosing to reinvest the revenue outperformance into growth initiatives (like marketing and card refreshes) rather than letting it drop to the bottom line or using it for share buybacks. Amex's credit quality remains pristine, with falling delinquencies and flat write-offs.

The City Angle: This is a classic conflict between short-term market expectations and long-term corporate strategy. Amex's premium strategy (younger consumers flocking to the Platinum card) is working, and reinvesting the beat to capture more high-spending Gen Z and Millennial Platinum cardholders is exactly what a long-term investor should want, even if it misses the quarterly buyback model.

items: What to say at work: 'The selloff in Amex is a classic case of the Street throwing a tantrum because management chose long-term growth over short-term buybacks. Spending is up 9.4% and credit quality is improving. Reinvesting the beat to capture more high-spending Gen Z and Millennial Platinum cardholders is exactly what a long-term investor should want.'

sections.title: Markets Briefing: What Moved and Why

content.text: If you spent Friday hoping for a quiet slide into the weekend, the markets had other plans. It was a classic tug-of-war session: the S&P 500 drifted up a microscopic 0.05% to close at 7,411.98, the Dow clawed back some of Thursday's losses to finish up 0.46% at 51,947.25, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq slipped another 0.64% to 24,975.82. Under the hood, the narrative is shifting fast. We are transitioning from the 'AI is going to save the world' phase to the 'who is actually paying for all these microchips, and when do we see the cash?' phase. Toss in a fresh geopolitical flare-up in the Middle East and Donald Trump’s latest midnight tariff magic trick, and you’ve got a cross-asset cocktail that’s keeping macro desks very awake.
The AI Capex Hangover: Intel’s Bitter Victory

The absolute poster child for Friday’s market mood was Intel. On Thursday night, the chipmaker dropped a blowout Q2 report: revenue up 25% year-over-year to $16.1 billion (its fastest growth in 15 years), driven by insatiable demand for server CPUs to power agentic AI. They also raised their annual capital expenditure forecast to $20 billion. Premarket, the stock was up 6%. By the closing bell? It was down 7.9% to $92.32. Why the brutal U-turn? Because the market looked at that $20 billion capex bill, started worrying about foundry customer pipeline execution, and realized Intel might have to dilute shareholders to fund the buildout. It’s the exact same script we saw with Alphabet and Tesla earlier in the week: hyperscaler spending is massive, but Wall Street’s patience for unmonetized capex is wearing thin. If you're in asset management, the trade is no longer just 'buy chipmakers'; it's 'show me the free cash flow'.
Trump’s Midnight Tariff Trick

Just as his temporary 10% global tariff under Section 122 was set to expire at midnight on Friday, President Trump pulled a classic legal rabbit out of his hat. To bypass the Supreme Court’s February ruling against his executive trade overreach, the administration slapped a fresh round of 10% to 12.5% tariffs on 60 to 80 global trading partners. This time, they used Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, weaponizing 'forced labor' investigations to cover nearly 100% of US imports. This comes on the heels of a massive 50% tariff slapped on Canadian goods earlier in the week. For the UK, Keir Starmer’s hard-won 10% exemption from last year holds, but it leaves British exporters in a weird spot as the EU secures slightly better terms. The cross-asset read here is simple: structural inflation is back on the menu, and supply chain re-shoring is about to get even more expensive.
The US-Iran War and Oil’s Brief Respite

Geopolitics continues to dictate the terms of the energy market. The US-Iran war escalated further on Friday, with US Central Command disabling a commercial tanker that repeatedly tried to run the blockade on Iranian ports, prompting Tehran to launch retaliatory drone strikes on US bases in Jordan and Kuwait. Brent crude, which had spiked past $102 a barrel on Thursday, eased back by nearly 4% to settle at $96.78. This minor pullback in energy costs was the only reason the Dow managed to put on a green face on Friday. But don’t let the daily dip fool you: with gold sitting at a staggering $4,056.30, the market is pricing in a massive, permanent geopolitical risk premium. Safe havens are expensive because the world is genuinely volatile.
The UK Angle: Burnham’s 'No10 North' and the BoE’s Dilemma

Back home, Andy Burnham has had a frantic first week as Prime Minister. On Friday, he officially opened 'No10 North' in Manchester, a symbolic move to decentralize economic policy away from Whitehall. He’s already throwing cash at the cost-of-living crisis, cutting business rates for hospitality and removing domestic electricity taxes. Coincidentally, UK PMIs bounced back strongly on Friday, with the composite index rising to 52.1 (the first growth in three months). But here’s the rub: while domestic business activity is looking up, the global energy shock is threatening to push UK inflation back to 3.5% this autumn. The Bank of England meets next week, and while they’ll likely hold rates, the market is now pricing in 45bps of hikes before the year is out. If you’re prepping for fixed-income interviews, the narrative is clear: fiscal easing from the new PM plus geopolitical energy shocks equals a very hawkish corner for the BoE.

content.text: The WACC Fallacy: Why Group Hurdle Rates Destroy Value

Imagine you are the CFO of a boring, rock-solid water utility. Your business is as safe as houses, your beta is a sleepy 0.6, and your Weighted Average Cost of Capital (WACC) is a comfortable 6%. But you are bored of water pipes. You want to get into the AI-powered SaaS game. You set up a new tech division, which, if it were a standalone business, would have a beta of 1.8 and a true cost of capital of 12%. When evaluating whether to fund a new AI project, which discount rate do you use? If you said 'our corporate WACC of 6%,' congratulations—you have just fallen headfirst into the WACC Fallacy.
The Concept: Hurdle Rates are About the Asset, Not the Owner

The WACC Fallacy is the corporate finance equivalent of using a ruler calibrated in centimetres to measure a football pitch and then wondering why the grass looks so long. It is the mistake of using a single, company-wide discount rate to evaluate all projects, divisions, or acquisitions, regardless of their individual risk profiles. In textbook theory, the discount rate for any investment should reflect the risk of that specific investment's cash flows, not the average risk of the company doing the investing. Yet, surveys show that over half of major corporations still use a single group-wide hurdle rate for everything they do.
The Math: How to Destroy Value in Two Easy Steps

Let us look at how this plays out in a spreadsheet. Suppose our utility-turned-tech conglomerate, 'Thames & Tech PLC', has a blended corporate WACC of 7% (heavily weighted by the massive utility side). The AI division proposes a project that requires £10 million today and is expected to return £11 million in Year 1 (a 10% nominal return).

items: The Correct Way: The AI project is high-risk, so we should discount it at the division's true cost of capital of 12%. NPV = (£11m / 1.12) - £10m = -£178,571. The NPV is negative. We reject the project. Correct decision.

The WACC Fallacy Way: We use the group WACC of 7%. NPV = (£11m / 1.07) - £10m = +£280,374. The NPV is positive! We pop the champagne, greenlight the project, and proceed to destroy £178k of shareholder value because we underpriced the risk.

content.text: The inverse is also true. If a high-risk tech firm (WACC of 12%) wants to build a super-safe data centre with a guaranteed 8% return (true cost of capital of 6%), using its group WACC of 12% will make the project look like a dog. They will reject a safe, value-creating project because their internal hurdle rate is artificially inflated by their core business risk.
Why It Matters in Asset Management and M&A

This is not just an academic nitpick. A landmark paper by Philipp Krüger, Augustin Landier, and David Thesmar published in the Journal of Finance ('The WACC Fallacy: The Real Effects of Using a Unique Discount Rate') proved that this bias leads to massive real-world capital misallocation. They found that conglomerates systematically overinvest in high-beta (risky) divisions and underinvest in low-beta (safe) divisions.

In M&A, the WACC Fallacy is a primary driver of overpaying for acquisitions. When a low-beta acquirer uses its own low WACC to discount the cash flows of a high-beta target, it overvalues the target and bids too high. The authors found that this mistake costs bidders, on average, about 0.8% of their market equity in diversifying deals—which equates to roughly 8% of the total deal value literally thrown down the drain.
How to Ace This in an Interview
If you are interviewing for investment banking, private equity, or buy-side roles, this is a classic trap question. The interviewer might ask:
"If a low-risk supermarket chain with a WACC of 6% is looking to acquire a high-growth, high-risk software startup, what discount rate should they use to value the startup's cash flows?"

The rookie mistake is to say '6%, because that is the acquirer's cost of capital.' The correct answer is: 'They must use the cost of capital of the target startup (or a peer group of software startups), not their own. WACC is a function of the risk of the cash flows being acquired, not the entity doing the acquiring. If they use 6%, they will underprice the risk, overvalue the startup, and overpay.'
Over a Pint: What to Say at the Pub

"It is wild how many corporate boards still use a single group hurdle rate. They end up starving their cash cows to fund speculative bets because the spreadsheet says the high-risk project has a higher NPV at the group WACC. It is literally a machine for destroying shareholder value, and it explains why so many diversifying acquisitions end up in massive write-downs a few years later."

sections.title: Quant / AI Finance Idea of the Day

content.text: 0.06 Sharpe vs. 1.99 Sharpe: The Mixed-Frequency Macro Trap

Let’s talk about a classic quant trap. You have daily price data, and you have monthly macroeconomic data (inflation, GDP, unemployment). You want your deep learning model to be 'macro-aware' so it doesn't get caught on the wrong side of a regime shift. The rookie move? Forward-fill the monthly macro data to daily, concatenate it with your price features, and feed the whole lot into an LSTM. Congratulations, you’ve just built a model with a spectacular 0.06 Sharpe ratio—worse than ignoring macro altogether.

Why does this happen? Deep neural networks are lazy. If you give them a slow-moving, forward-filled macro feature, they will happily overfit to those static values, treating them as rigid 'states' rather than learning the underlying dynamics. When the out-of-sample regime shifts, the model collapses.
The Solution: Hierarchical Attention Networks (HANET)

A paper from the Oxford-Man Institute of Quantitative Finance (Oliveira et al., May 2026) introduces HANET (Hierarchical Attention Network). Instead of naive feature concatenation, HANET organizes information in a hierarchical mixed-frequency structure. Daily asset returns are nested within monthly macroeconomic windows, and a Hierarchical Cross-Attention mechanism reconciles the low-frequency macro signals with high-frequency returns without discarding granular daily information.

By framing regime selection as attention over macroeconomic contexts, the model acts like a human macro trader. It treats the current high-frequency market state as a 'query' and searches across a 'key-value' store of historical monthly macro regimes to find analogous periods. For example, during the COVID-19 crash in 2020, the model naturally leaned on its memory of the 2008 financial crisis. During the 2022 inflation spike, it reached back to the early-1980s Volcker era. This structured conditioning yielded a massive 1.99 Sharpe ratio on time-series momentum tasks across 55 liquid futures.
A Toy PyTorch Implementation

import torch
import torch.nn as nn

class HierarchicalMacroAttention(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, daily_dim, macro_dim, embed_dim):
        super().__init__()
        # Project current daily market features (Query)
        self.q_proj = nn.Linear(daily_dim, embed_dim)
        # Project historical monthly macro features (Keys and Values)
        self.k_proj = nn.Linear(macro_dim, embed_dim)
        self.v_proj = nn.Linear(macro_dim, embed_dim)
        self.scale = embed_dim ** -0.5
        
    def forward(self, daily_state, macro_history):
        # daily_state: [batch, daily_dim] (current market context)
        # macro_history: [batch, num_months, macro_dim] (historical macro regimes)
        
        # 1. Generate Query, Keys, and Values
        Q = self.q_proj(daily_state).unsqueeze(1) # [batch, 1, embed_dim]
        K = self.k_proj(macro_history)            # [batch, num_months, embed_dim]
        V = self.v_proj(macro_history)            # [batch, num_months, embed_dim]
        
        # 2. Compute attention weights (matching current state to past macro regimes)
        attn_scores = torch.bmm(Q, K.transpose(1, 2)) * self.scale # [batch, 1, num_months]
        attn_weights = torch.softmax(attn_scores, dim=-1)
        
        # 3. Retrieve the blended macro context
        macro_context = torch.bmm(attn_weights, V).squeeze(1) # [batch, embed_dim]
        
        # 4. Combine daily state with the retrieved macro context
        combined = torch.cat([daily_state, macro_context], dim=-1)
        return combined, attn_weights
How to Use This in an Interview or at the Pub

items: The Rookie Mistake: If an interviewer asks how you'd integrate macro indicators (monthly/quarterly) with daily trading data, do not say 'I'd forward-fill it and throw it in an XGBoost.' Explain that naive upsampling causes severe overfitting because the model treats the static, repeated macro values as rigid states.

The Pro Answer: Pitch the concept of Hierarchical Cross-Attention. Explain that you want to represent the current market state as a 'query' and search across a 'key-value' store of historical macro regimes to find analogous periods (e.g., matching 2022's inflation to the 1980s). This preserves the temporal structure of macro history.

The Killer Stat: Mention that shuffling the temporal order of the macro history in this architecture collapses the Sharpe ratio from 1.99 to 0.81. This proves that the model isn't just memorizing static macro values; it is actually leveraging the sequential, temporal structure of macroeconomic regimes.

content.text: The Catch: Risks and Limitations

items: Lookahead Bias & Revisions: Macroeconomic data (like GDP or inflation) is heavily revised after its initial release. If you train your model on 'revised' historical data, you are introducing lookahead bias. You must use 'point-in-time' (vintage) macro data to reflect what the market actually knew at that moment.

The 'This Time is Different' Risk: If the market enters a completely unprecedented regime (e.g., a novel geopolitical shock or a unique monetary policy experiment), the attention mechanism will be forced to distribute weights across poor historical matches, potentially leading to erratic trading signals.

Computational Overhead: While compressing the history to monthly intervals helps, performing cross-attention over decades of historical regimes still adds significant computational complexity compared to simple feedforward or recurrent networks.

sections.title: One Article or Paper Worth Reading

content.text: The Paper: The max EPS Paradigm for Corporate Finance

If you have ever sat through a corporate finance lecture on Modigliani-Miller or the Weighted Average Cost of Capital (WACC), only to walk into an investment bank or asset manager and find everyone staring blankly at an accretion/dilution model, you have experienced the grand canyon of finance. Academics love to sniff at corporate executives who obsess over Earnings Per Share (EPS), calling it short-termist or irrational. But a brilliant NBER working paper by Itzhak Ben-David and Alex Chinco, titled The max EPS Paradigm for Corporate Finance (NBER WP 34971, March 2026), does something radical: it treats the real world with respect. Instead of dismissing EPS maximization as a mistake, they formalise it into a rigorous, mathematically consistent framework that actually explains corporate behaviour far better than traditional academic models.
Why This One Matters

For decades, the academic consensus has been that capital structure is irrelevant (without taxes and frictions) and that companies should only care about Net Present Value (NPV) using risk-adjusted discount rates. Meanwhile, CFOs and investment bankers spend their lives looking at whether a deal is accretive or dilutive to EPS. Ben-David and Chinco show that if you assume a CEO's actual goal is simply to maximize EPS, you get a beautiful, unified theory of corporate finance that explains capital structure, capital budgeting, and payout policy in one go—without needing to invent complex market frictions.
The Core Idea: Growth vs. Value

The model's magic lies in how it defines the earnings cost of different capital sources. The earnings cost of equity is simply the firm's earnings yield (EY, which is E/P, or the inverse of the P/E ratio). The earnings cost of debt is the interest rate on the next dollar borrowed. By comparing a firm's earnings yield to the risk-free rate, the authors draw a bright line between two types of firms:

items: Growth Stocks (EY < rf): Their earnings yield is below the risk-free rate. Because their equity is so expensive (high P/E, low EY), they see equity as incredibly cheap. They remain unlevered, hoard cash, and never return cash to shareholders because they can easily clear their low earnings-yield hurdle by investing in risk-free bonds.

Value Stocks (EY > rf): Their earnings yield is above the risk-free rate. They see risk-free debt as cheap relative to their equity. They lever up, repurchase shares, and return cash when they cannot find high-yield projects to beat their high hurdle rate.

content.text: The Three Pillars of the Max EPS Paradigm

items: Capital Structure: CEOs lever up when creditors want less earnings than shareholders for the marginal dollar. This delivers an optimal leverage ratio even in a frictionless world—no need to balance tax shields against bankruptcy costs.

Capital Budgeting: Instead of positive NPV, EPS maximizers look for accretive projects where the project's income yield is higher than the firm's cheapest financing option. This explains why practitioners love IRR (which measures how accretive a project is) and payback periods (which express the income yield as a multiple).

Payout Policy: Holding cash has an opportunity cost equal to the firm's earnings yield. Deep value stocks are the most likely to return cash because they face a high hurdle, making cash retention expensive. They prefer buybacks because buybacks can be accretive, whereas dividends are neutral.

content.text: Key Quotes from the Paper

The max EPS approach delivers an optimal leverage ratio even in the absence of frictions, an investment rule based on comparing yields rather than using a risk-adjusted discount rate, and a payout policy where accretive buybacks are preferred to neutral dividends.

Growth stocks have earnings yields below the riskfree rate; value stocks have earnings yields above it. This single comparison leads the two kinds of firms to pursue different constellations of EPS-maximizing policies.
What to Skim and What to Read

You can safely skim the heavy mathematical proofs of the optimal leverage ratio in Section 1. But do not skim the sections on capital budgeting and payout policy. The explanation of why practitioners naturally gravitate toward IRR and payback periods—and why buybacks are structurally preferred to dividends by EPS maximizers—is pure gold.
How to Use This at Work or in an Interview

If you are interviewing for an investment banking or corporate finance role, this paper is a cheat code. When asked about capital structure or capital budgeting, you can show serious commercial awareness by bridging the gap between theory and practice. You can say:

While academic theory focuses on WACC and NPV, in practice, corporate managers are highly focused on EPS maximization. What is fascinating is that recent research by Ben-David and Chinco shows this isn't just a dumb heuristic. If you model EPS maximization directly, it perfectly explains why growth firms naturally hoard cash and value firms lever up to buy back shares, without needing to rely on market frictions.

Over a pint with colleagues, it is a great way to debate why the tech giants (classic growth) held massive cash piles for so long, and why the transition of mature tech companies into paying dividends or doing massive buybacks is a natural consequence of their earnings yields rising above the risk-free rate.

content.text: The Door-in-the-Face Technique: Why asking for the moon gets you the streetlamp

Imagine you are trying to get your Managing Director to agree to a Friday deadline for a beast of a financial model. If you walk in and ask for Friday, they will probably tell you they need it by Wednesday close of play. But if you walk in and ask for next Tuesday, they will scoff, tell you to pull your finger out, and you will "compromise" on Friday. Congratulations: you have just successfully executed the "Door-in-the-Face" (DITF) technique, one of the most reliable compliance hacks in social psychology.

First formalised by psychologist Robert Cialdini and his colleagues in a classic 1975 study, the DITF technique is the exact opposite of the "foot-in-the-door" approach. Instead of starting small, you start with an extreme, borderline-unreasonable request that you fully expect to get rejected (the metaphorical door slammed in your face). Once they say no, you immediately pivot to your actual, much more reasonable target request.

Cialdini proved this by sending researchers around a university campus posing as juvenile detention officers. When they asked students to chaperone juvenile delinquents on a two-hour trip to the zoo, only 17% agreed. But when they first asked students to volunteer as unpaid counsellors at the detention centre for two hours a week for two years (an extreme request that 100% of people rejected) and then asked them to chaperone the zoo trip, the agreement rate tripled to 50%. Crucially, a massive 2021 replication study by Oliver Genschow and his team at the University of Cologne confirmed that this effect is highly robust and holds up perfectly today.
Why does this work so well in the City? It relies on two powerful psychological levers:

items: The Norm of Reciprocity: When you lower your demands from "next Tuesday" to "this Friday", the other party perceives this as a personal concession. Human social programming dictates that when someone makes a concession to us, we feel an intense, almost subconscious urge to make a concession in return.
Perceptual Contrast: A Friday deadline looks incredibly tight in isolation. But compared to next Tuesday, it feels like a massive compromise that the MD has successfully extracted from you.

content.text: How to use it without looking like a sociopath
Like any powerful negotiation tool, if you overplay your hand, you will just look manipulative or completely out of touch. Here is how to deploy it in the wild:

items: Keep the first request plausible: If you ask for a £50k pay rise when the budget is £5k, your boss will just think you are delusional and the negotiation will collapse. The initial request must be ambitious but within the realm of physical possibility.

No delay between requests: The psychological magic of the concession only works if the second request is made immediately after the rejection. If you wait until the next day, the contrast effect fades, and they will just see it as two separate conversations.

Frame it as a concession: Use language that highlights your "compromise". Phrases like "Tell you what, if we strip out the secondary scenario analysis, I can get the core deck to you by Friday" work wonders because they make the other person feel like they have won.

content.text: Whether you are pitching advisory fees to a client, negotiating a budget with finance, or just trying to claw back your weekend from an overzealous VP, remember that starting with what you actually want is a rookie error.
If you want a small favour, ask for a massive one first. People hate saying 'no' twice.
